body:
Meaning and characteristics of puppetry

Puppetry is a performing art in which manipulated figures represent characters, animals, objects or imaginary beings. Puppeteers bring these figures to life through movement, speech, narration and music.

Traditional Indian puppetry communicates stories from epics, mythology, folklore, historical legends and social life. It combines the work of craftspeople, storytellers, musicians and performers.

Wood, leather, cloth and other materials may be used to make puppets. The material alone does not determine the category of puppetry. Its classification depends mainly on the way the puppet is manipulated or presented.

The 4 principal forms of Indian puppetry

  • String puppets: Figures suspended and manipulated by strings controlled from above.
  • Rod puppets: Figures supported and manipulated using rods.
  • Glove puppets: Figures fitted over the puppeteer's hand and moved through finger and hand movements.
  • Shadow puppets: Figures placed between a source of light and a screen so that their images or shadows become visible to the audience.

These categories identify the main characteristics of each form. Some traditions combine more than one method of manipulation, such as the use of both strings and rods.

String puppets

String puppets are also called marionettes. Their movements are produced through strings connected to different parts of the figure. They are particularly suitable for representing human characters, dance sequences and dramatic action.

Kathputli of Rajasthan

Kathputli is one of India's best-known string puppetry traditions. Its name combines Kath, meaning wood, and Putli, meaning doll or puppet.

The figures commonly have carved wooden heads, painted faces and colourful cloth costumes. Traditional female and male figures often have long flowing costumes that conceal the lower part of the body.

Kathputli has historically been associated with traditional Bhat or Bhatt puppeteer families of Rajasthan. Its performances include royal stories, historical legends, humorous scenes, heroic characters and entertainment for village or urban audiences.

Gombeyatta of Karnataka

Karnataka has a string puppetry tradition commonly called Gombeyatta. Yakshagana Sutrada Gombeyatta is closely associated with the stories, costumes and dramatic character types of Yakshagana.

The resemblance between puppet costumes and the costumes of human Yakshagana performers shows the relationship between puppet theatre and regional dance-drama.

Kundhei of Odisha

Kundhei, also associated with the name Sakhi Kundhei, is a traditional puppetry form of Odisha. Its string puppet tradition uses figures commonly made of light wood and dressed in regional costumes.

Odisha also possesses rod and shadow puppet traditions. Therefore, the word Kundhei, which refers broadly to dolls or puppets, must be interpreted with its particular descriptive name when identifying the puppet category.

Other string puppet traditions

FormStateIdentifying feature
Kalasutri BahulyaMaharashtraTraditional string puppets
BommalattamTamil NaduCombination of strings and rods

Bommalattam is especially useful for understanding the limits of rigid classification. Its traditional puppets may be supported and controlled through both strings and rods.

Rod puppets

Rod puppets are manipulated using rods attached to or supporting the figure. Rods may support the main body and control movements of the limbs.

Daanger Putul of West Bengal

West Bengal possesses a prominent rod puppet tradition known as Daanger Putul, also associated with Putul Nautch. The puppets are often relatively large and can be presented in dramatic performances influenced by Bengali folk theatre.

Putul Nautch broadly means puppet dance or puppet performance. Since Bengal has more than one puppet tradition, Daanger Putul is the more precise name for identifying its rod puppet form.

Yampuri of Bihar

Yampuri is a traditional rod puppetry form of Bihar. Its wooden puppets are associated with narratives concerning morality and the consequences of human actions.

Kathi Kundhei of Odisha

Kathi Kundhei is a rod puppetry tradition of Odisha. The distinctive descriptive name is useful for differentiating it from Odisha's string and shadow puppet forms.

Important form-state associations

Puppet traditionStateCategory
KathputliRajasthanString
Yakshagana Sutrada GombeyattaKarnatakaString
Sakhi KundheiOdishaString
Kalasutri BahulyaMaharashtraString
BommalattamTamil NaduString and rod
Daanger PutulWest BengalRod
YampuriBiharRod
Kathi KundheiOdishaRod

Prelims focus

  • The 4 principal puppet categories are string, rod, glove and shadow.
  • Kathputli: Rajasthan, string puppetry and traditional Bhat puppeteers.
  • Yakshagana Sutrada Gombeyatta: Karnataka, string puppetry.
  • Yampuri: Bihar; Daanger Putul: West Bengal; Kathi Kundhei: Odisha.
  • Kalasutri Bahulya is Maharashtra's string puppet tradition.
  • Trap: Bommalattam of Tamil Nadu can combine strings and rods.

[References: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Theatre Crafts, pp. 112 and 116; CCRT, The Art of Puppetry, Parts 1 and 2, sections on string and rod puppets; Ministry of Culture, Indicative List of Folk, Traditional and Indigenous Art; Development Commissioner for Handicrafts, Craft Processes and Other Details of 32 Crafts, Theatre, Costumes and Puppet section; Rajasthan Government, Handmade in Rajasthan, Kathputli; Ministry of Communications, PIB release on Puppets of India, 14 February 2026; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Indian Puppetry: Classification, String Puppets and Rod Puppets

body:
Shadow puppetry

Shadow puppetry is a theatrical form in which figures are placed between a source of light and a screen. The audience views the projected shadows or coloured images of the figures rather than directly watching their manipulation.

Traditional Indian shadow puppets are commonly made from processed leather. Some traditions use translucent coloured figures, while others use opaque figures that create dark silhouettes.

The projected image may represent an individual character, animal, landscape feature or other element of a story. Music and narration accompany the visual performance.

Important shadow puppet traditions

Tholu Bommalata of Andhra Pradesh

Tholu Bommalata, also written as Tolu Bommalatta, is a major shadow puppetry tradition of Andhra Pradesh. Its name refers to leather puppets and their performance.

The figures are generally large, flat and made from translucent coloured leather. When illuminated behind a screen, they produce colourful images. The Ramayana and Mahabharata are important sources of their stories.

Togalu Gombeyatta of Karnataka

Togalu Gombeyatta is Karnataka's traditional leather shadow puppetry. The word Togalu refers to leather.

It should be distinguished from Karnataka's Sutrada Gombeyatta, which is a string puppet tradition. Both belong to Karnataka, but their categories of puppetry are different.

Ravanachhaya of Odisha

Ravanachhaya is a shadow puppetry tradition of Odisha. It is particularly associated with narratives from the Ramayana.

Its traditional leather figures are comparatively small, opaque and generally without movable joints. They produce dark silhouettes rather than the coloured projected images characteristic of translucent Andhra Pradesh puppets.

Tholpavakoothu of Kerala

Tholpavakoothu, also written as Thol Pavakoothu, is a ritual shadow puppetry tradition of Kerala. It has a strong connection with Bhagavati temples, particularly in the Palakkad region.

Its traditional narrative draws upon the Ramayana, especially the Tamil version associated with Kamban. The performance combines ritual observance, recitation, music and leather shadow figures.

Kerala also has glove puppetry traditions with similar names. The prefix Thol, referring to leather, is a useful identifying element of Tholpavakoothu.

Other shadow puppet traditions

Tamil Nadu also has a traditional leather shadow puppet form commonly known as Thol Bommalattam or Thol Pavai Koothu. Maharashtra's Chamadyache Bahulya is another regional shadow puppet tradition.

FormPrincipal stateIdentifying feature
Tholu BommalataAndhra PradeshLarge translucent coloured figures
Togalu GombeyattaKarnatakaLeather shadow puppets
RavanachhayaOdishaOpaque silhouettes
TholpavakoothuKeralaTemple-based ritual shadow theatre
Thol BommalattamTamil NaduLeather shadow puppets
Chamadyache BahulyaMaharashtraRegional leather shadow puppetry

Glove puppetry

Glove puppets are worn directly over the puppeteer's hand. The movement of fingers and the hand controls the puppet's head and arms. They are comparatively portable and can be used in small performance spaces.

Pavakathakali of Kerala

Pavakathakali, also associated with the name Pavakoothu, is a glove puppetry tradition of Kerala influenced by Kathakali.

Its figures resemble Kathakali performers in their painted faces, colourful costumes and decorative headgear. The characters and narratives commonly draw upon epic and religious stories.

Pavakathakali is a form of glove puppetry, whereas Tholpavakoothu is shadow puppetry. Both are associated with Kerala.

Gulabo Sitabo of Uttar Pradesh

Gulabo Sitabo is a traditional glove puppet form of Uttar Pradesh. Its presentation is associated with humorous dialogue, familiar social situations and entertainment.

Benir Putul of West Bengal

Benir Putul is a traditional glove puppetry form of West Bengal. It should be distinguished from Daanger Putul, the rod puppet form of the same state.

Glove puppetry is also practised in other regions, including Odisha. A particular state may therefore possess several different puppet traditions.

Commemorative postage stamps on Puppets of India

On 13 February 2026, the Department of Posts released a set of 8 commemorative postage stamps titled Puppets of India at the India Habitat Centre, New Delhi.

The issue represented the 4 principal puppet categories through the following regional traditions:

CategoryTraditions represented
StringKathputli, Rajasthan; Yakshagana Sutrada Gombeyatta, Karnataka
RodDaanger Putul, West Bengal; Kathi Kundhei, Odisha
GloveBenir Putul, West Bengal; Pavakathakali, Kerala
ShadowRavanachhaya, Odisha; Tolu Bommalatta, Andhra Pradesh

This was a completed commemorative issue, as recorded in the official Ministry of Communications release dated 14 February 2026. The selected 8 traditions represent examples of Indian puppetry rather than an exhaustive national classification.

Prelims focus

  • Tholu Bommalata: Andhra Pradesh; Togalu Gombeyatta: Karnataka; Ravanachhaya: Odisha.
  • Tholpavakoothu is Kerala's ritual shadow puppetry tradition.
  • Pavakathakali is Kerala's Kathakali-influenced glove puppetry.
  • Gulabo Sitabo: Uttar Pradesh, glove puppetry.
  • Benir Putul: West Bengal, glove puppetry.
  • Trap: Karnataka's Togalu Gombeyatta uses shadow figures, whereas Sutrada Gombeyatta uses string puppets.

[References: NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Theatre Crafts, p. 116; CCRT, The Art of Puppetry, Parts 1 and 2, sections on shadow and glove puppets; Ministry of Culture, Indicative List of Folk, Traditional and Indigenous Art; Development Commissioner for Handicrafts, Craft Processes and Other Details of 32 Crafts, Theatre, Costumes and Puppet section; Ministry of Communications, PIB, Department of Posts Releases Set of 8 Commemorative Postage Stamps on Puppets of India, 14 February 2026, Release ID 2227936; consulted 26 November 2026.]

title: Shadow Puppetry, Glove Puppetry and Regional Distinctions

body:
Oral tradition and the transmission of stories

An oral tradition is a cultural tradition in which stories, songs, knowledge and customs are transmitted substantially through speech, recitation, singing or performance.

Before the widespread availability of printed material, travelling storytellers, bards, religious performers and village artists played an important role in preserving and communicating knowledge.

Oral traditions do not necessarily lack written texts. A story may exist in written manuscripts, printed books and oral performance at the same time. Performers may adapt the narrative to their regional language, audience and cultural setting.

Epics as sources of storytelling

An epic is an extended narrative concerning heroic figures, major events, social values or religious and mythological themes.

The Ramayana and Mahabharata are among the most influential sources of Indian storytelling. Their stories have been adapted into literary works, songs, theatrical performances, puppetry and painted scrolls.

Different communities may preserve their own versions of an epic. These versions can include changes in emphasis, additional characters and local cultural references while retaining connections with the wider narrative tradition.

Other important sources of oral storytelling include Puranic narratives, stories of regional heroes, local deities, historical legends and accounts of community life.

Pandavani of Chhattisgarh

Pandavani is a musical and dramatic storytelling tradition particularly associated with Chhattisgarh. Its name refers to the stories of the Pandavas.

The narrator presents episodes from the Mahabharata using song, recitation, expressive gestures and dramatic narration. A leading performer is commonly accompanied by supporting musicians.

The tradition is historically associated with communities including the Pardhan, Gond and Dewar communities.

Two important styles of Pandavani are Vedamati and Kapalika. The Vedamati style is associated with a more text-oriented and relatively restrained narration, whereas Kapalika is more dramatic and expressive.

Teejan Bai is a celebrated exponent of the Kapalika style. Her performances helped bring Pandavani to national and international audiences.

Pandavani is a tradition of musical and dramatic oral narration. It is not a category of puppetry, even though it shares epic narratives with puppet theatre.

Phad storytelling of Rajasthan

Phad is a painted narrative scroll tradition of Rajasthan. It combines visual art with oral performance and commonly presents the stories of legendary heroes and local religious figures.

Important Phad narratives concern Pabuji and Devnarayan. Their stories are preserved through large painted cloth scrolls and musical narration.

Traditional narrators are known as Bhopas. The female performing partner is commonly called a Bhopi. The scroll is displayed during the performance, and the performers narrate or sing the stories represented in its painted scenes.

The Phad traditionally serves not only as a visual aid but also as a portable sacred object. Its cultural importance therefore includes painting, oral literature, music and community worship.

Painted scroll storytelling in other regions

In Bengal, traditional singer-painters known as Patuas or Chitrakars narrate stories using painted scrolls. As the scroll is progressively revealed, the performer sings or explains the corresponding scenes.

Although religious stories form an important part of this tradition, painted scroll storytelling has also been adapted to historical events, natural disasters and contemporary social subjects.

Cheriyal scroll storytelling of Telangana is another example of the connection between painted narrative traditions and oral performance.

Other important storytelling forms

FormPrincipal regionIdentifying feature
HarikathaSeveral southern Indian regionsDevotional storytelling with music and religious interpretation
BurrakathaAndhra Pradesh and TelanganaMusical narration supported by accompanying performers
VillupattuTamil NaduStorytelling accompanied by a musical bow
PandavaniChhattisgarhMusical narration of Mahabharata episodes
PhadRajasthanOral narration using painted cloth scrolls

Distinguishing the medium from the narrative

Several performance traditions tell the same story through different media. A Mahabharata episode may be presented by live actors in Yakshagana, narrated by a Pandavani singer or represented through leather shadow puppets.

The source narrative alone does not determine the name of a performing art. The performers, region, instruments, presentation and medium must also be considered.

Prelims focus

  • Pandavani: Chhattisgarh, Mahabharata and Teejan Bai.
  • Vedamati and Kapalika are styles of Pandavani.
  • Phad: Rajasthan, Bhopas and Bhopis, Pabuji and Devnarayan.
  • Patuas: painted scroll storytellers of Bengal.
  • Burrakatha: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana; Villupattu: Tamil Nadu.
  • Trap: Phad is painted-scroll narration, not shadow puppetry.

[References: NCERT, Our Pasts-I, Class 6, 2018–19 edition, Buildings, Paintings and Books, pp. 127–130; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, Painting and Theatre Crafts, pp. 112 and 121; IGNCA, Pandavani Chhattisgarh, documentary description; IGNCA, Phad: Scroll Paintings and Their Narration, Rajasthan, Intangible Cultural Heritage collection; National Cultural Audiovisual Archives, Pandavani Performance by Ms. Teejan Bai, recording dated 28 February 1987; Ministry of Culture, Indicative List of Folk, Traditional and Indigenous Art; online sources consulted 26 November 2026.]
